abstract: Perceptually-based linear predictive (PLP) speech analysis, as proposed by Hermansky 1985, can have marked benefits in ASR (automatic speech recognition) systems. Four psychoacoustic factors are considered in PLP analysis, namely critical-band, masking effect, equal-loudness and intensity-loudness law. This paper presents experimental results aimed at illustrating the relative importance of each of these in the context of ASR. It is shown that the (J) SRU filter bank can be incorporated into the PLP process with very similar overall results. The ASR system is based on dynamic time warping (DTW), and a vocabulary consisting of the alphabet and zero-through-nine is used for tests.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Formant extraction from group delay function
abstract: A new approach to the extraction of formant information from speech signals is presented. The method exploits the additive and high resolution properties of group delay functions to resolve even closely spaced formants. The group delay function (or the negative derivative of Fourier transform phase) is derived for a minimum phase signal, which in turn is derived from the Fourier transform magnitude of the speech signal. The method is shown to give highly consistent estimation of formants without resorting to any modelling approach for smoothing the magnitude spectrum.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Improving speech synthesis by analysis by rule
abstract: This paper is concerned with details of the adaption process: a method of speech-analysis-by-synthesis-by-rule ('analysis-by-rule') which provides the parameters of an underlying speech production model from an analysis of natural speech. This process is considered as a useful technique in its own right for analysing the acoustic realisations of a phonetic segment sequence. In particular, this paper addresses the question of acoustic variability and demonstrates that the analysis technique can separate predictable changes in segment realisation due to phonetic context from unpredictable changes due to variability in articulation, environment or analysis. In their original proposal Bridle and Ralls (1985) use a least-squares fitting technique to fit their SbR model to a corpus of natural speech to obtain the best data table values. This can be seen to confuse the two types of variability; whilst random variability can be captured as probability density functions for the data table values, the contextual variability requires changed to the rule-structure of the synthesis system.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Optimum design of running Fourier transform filter banks
abstract: For spectral analysis the running Fourier transform filter bank outlined in this paper has zero phase distortion, and can be designed to have minimal; amplitude distortion with the aid of an 'equivalent' composite impulse response plot. Resolution, analysing bandwidth and filter roll-off are independently variable so as to minimise spectral leakage. For spectral analysis-synthesis, the location of the main pulse in the composite impulse response can be altered independently of the other parameters so as to minimise composite amplitude and phase ripple. It is also possible to optimally design filter banks with non-linear channel spacing and semi-variable analysing bandwidth.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A Chebyshev transform: A new transform with particular application to speech
abstract: The limited results presented tend to support the contention that the combination of the cosine sampling law and the associated Chebyshev transform offer a particularly good combination of sampling law and sub-optimum orthogonal transform ion the particular case of speech data. However, the results give only a qualitative indication that the new Chebyshev transform is particularly relevant for speech data but suggest that it is at least worthy of further investigation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A model for optimising the size of speech parcels for use on packet switched networks carrying real time interactive speech
abstract: An initial hardware/software model has been developed to assess the ability of a local area network (LAN) employing the Technical Office Protocol (TOP-IEEE 802.3), to carry interactive speech while heavily loaded with data traffic. The intelligibility of the speech is subjectively assessed for both unidirectional and bidirectional transmissions. The packet structure of CSMA/CD network being used is such that the minimum data packet size is 46 bytes. In the interests of efficiency, successive speech sample (packets) have been grouped together in parcels and loaded into the data section of the CSMA/CD frame for transmission. Subjective results have been obtained as to the optimum parcel size for reasonable user acceptability.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Acoustic-phonetic attribute determination using multi-layer perceptrons
abstract: The multi-layer perceptron (MP) provides a means of performing complex pattern recognition and feature detection tasks. It is capable of implementing non-linear transformations which may be found by means of an iterative training procedure, known at the generalized delta rule. Such a technique is therefore of particular interest in determining elementary phonetic attributes of the speech signal, as first results suggest. This paper describes the application of an MLP network to the feature-labelling of simple speech material. The output of the network is a feature vector for each input time-window. The network can be viewed as either a pre-processing stage for a phonetic recognition system, or simply as a non-linear data reduction of the signal for input to pattern-matching recognisers.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

Currently the two most popular speech analysis by synthesis coding techniques are multi-pulse linear predictive coding (MP-LPC) and code excited linear prediction (CELP). Much of the recent work on CELP has been concentrated on complexity reduction and improved quantisation of the LPC filter. This paper focuses on a new complexity reduction technique for CELP coders employing sparse vector codebooks.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Speech analysis and recognition using a feature-based weighted scoring mechanism
abstract: A simple scoring mechanism has been developed for speech recognition purposes. In analysis mode (common to both training and recognition processing), peak patterns are obtained from each 10 ms frame of channel values from a 15-channel analog filter bank. In addition, tests are made for the presence of certain high-level speech features such as nasality, unvoiced speech etc. Scoring is based on matching input peak patterns and features against stored patterns and features. Successful matching results in the score associated with a particular peak pattern or feature being added to an accumulated score. Weightings are used to discriminate between features and peak patterns and between peak patterns.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Application of speech technology in the automotive industry
abstract: Provides an insight into some of the current applications of speech technology in the industrial sector. Some specific examples from the authors own experience are discussed in detail. The scope of speech technology as a tool for human computer interaction is widely acknowledged. However, it is comparatively recently that the reliability and cost of such systems has reached a level where this technology can be considered for applications outside the laboratory, in particular in the hostile environment of the industrial shop-floor. It is the aim of this paper to describe the currently perceived limitations of the technology for this type of application, and further to describe two applications where the technology is being used in anger.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
